item.title: Zelensky: U.S. pushing energy ceasefire, trilateral talks with Russia
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The Trump administration is pushing for three immediate steps in its effort to de-escalate the war in Ukraine and restart diplomacy with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview on Wednesday: A ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Reopening the Black Sea grain corridor. A trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting, possibly in Abu Dhabi. Why it matters: President Trump is engaged in a renewed effort to revive a diplomatic track to end the war, but his immediate priority is a deal to halt Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel fuel — which have contributed to punishing prices in the U.S. and globally. But after several days of diplomacy and meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week, an energy ceasefire looks elusive. It's unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin even wants it. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev will arrive in New York on Thursday for a meeting with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to discuss the latest U.S. proposals, according to a source with direct knowledge. Driving the news: Zelensky spoke with Trump on Tuesday in New York about efforts to end the war and a possible energy ceasefire. Later on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner met with Ukraine's negotiations team and the national security advisers of France, the UK and Germany. Zelensky told Axios the proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure came from the U.S. and that Ukraine is ready to agree. "On the table now there is a proposition: energy ceasefire. We are ready," he said. Zelensky added that the U.S. is also seeking to reopen the grain corridor and convene a trilateral meeting between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia. Zoom in: The last U.S.-Ukraine-Russia meeting took place in February before the war with Iran. Since then, negotiations have gone into a deep freeze. Zelensky said he told Trump he would prefer to hold a trilateral meeting and make an energy ceasefire one of its first concrete outcomes. The U.S. raised the possibility of first holding a meeting between technical teams, as opposed to a meeting at the leaders level. It floated Abu Dhabi as a possible venue, Zelensky said. "We are open — any country, any format," he said. The Ukrainian president said he told Trump during their meeting that December's G20 summit in Miami could also be an opportunity for a leader-level trilateral summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that Trump invited Putin to attend the summit. Zelensky also said simply getting the three sides into the same room would itself be a significant step toward de-escalation. Catch up quick: The current push for resuming negotiations started three weeks ago when CIA director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow. It was followed by Witkoff and Kushner traveling to Moscow and Kyiv. They met Putin for three hours in Moscow on Sept. 5 and then traveled to Kyiv to meet Zelensky. After they returned, Trump had a long phone call with Putin. Behind the scenes: Zelensky said Witkoff and Kushner were very optimistic when they briefed him after meeting with Putin. "They said, 'We think that Putin is ready.' I said, 'Look, I'm not sure,'" Zelensky recalled. According to Zelensky, the U.S. envoys responded: "No, we are close." Zelensky said he told them he was ready to discuss an energy ceasefire and other de-escalation steps but remained skeptical Putin would follow through. Yes, but: Zelensky said he continues to doubt Putin's intentions and believes the Russian leader could find reasons to avoid a trilateral meeting with leaders present. On Wednesday, the Kremlin said the conditions aren't ready for resuming peace talks with Ukraine and that there is no prospect at the moment for high-level meetings between the parties. Minutes before Zelensky spoke to Axios, Russia launched multiple ballistic missiles toward Kyiv. Zelensky received several updates on his phone about the additional missile attacks throughout the interview. What they're saying: Zelensky said Trump was "very positive" about the diplomatic push during their meeting Tuesday. Trump told him, "We will try," Zelensky said. "I said, 'Great, and really wish you not only to try [but] to succeed,'" Zelensky recalled. Zelensky stressed that Kyiv wants progress before winter sets in, regardless of the U.S. political calendar. Between the lines: The U.S. has its own economic interest in an energy ceasefire. Zelensky said American officials told him that reducing attacks on energy infrastructure was important because of the impact on energy prices. State of play: Zelensky said he spoke Tuesday with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and officials from India, the UAE and Egypt about the ceasefire effort and reopening the grain corridor. Those countries are also talking to Russia, he said. "Everybody wants [a] ceasefire. The corridor has to work again. We support [it]. They speak with Russians, I know. We will see," Zelensky said. What's next: Zelensky said Witkoff, Kushner and his team held follow-up talks after his meeting with Trump and agreed to continue working on the proposals and convey messages to Moscow. Ukrainian officials said some elements still need to be developed over the next two weeks before the Americans take them back to the Russians. Zelensky said he expects Trump to focus first on trying to secure the energy ceasefire.

item.title: "We have a choice": AI leaders sound alarm at UN
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Executives from leading artificial intelligence organizations urged global cooperation Wednesday to address risks from increasingly autonomous AI systems during a UN Security Council meeting. The big picture: AI capabilities are advancing faster than governments are developing safeguards, raising concerns about whether humans can maintain control over increasingly autonomous systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared in person at the meeting, while Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue joined by video conference. Driving the news: " We have a choice in front of us," Altman said. "AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray." He outlined the risks of AI systems becoming increasingly autonomous, warning "they could move faster than our institutions, concentrate power in too few hands, or make decisions that people no longer understand or control," fears he noted become increasingly urgent as AI systems move toward self-improvement . "It doesn't matter whether people put the risk of catastrophe at 10% or 1% or 12% or 0.1 percent," he said. "None of these levels are remotely acceptable, and we should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we'll be able to keep under human control." State of play: A recent Hugging Face breach and newly disclosed AI safety incidents have intensified concerns about monitoring and security standards. The UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warned that the present AI firewalls are "unravelling." Last week, OpenAI disclosed six new incidents where its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials or committed other misbehaviors — making it clear the Hugging Face breach was an eye-opener, not a standalone fluke, Axios previously reported. " To better understand and mitigate these emerging cybersecurity risks, the global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure," Delangue said Wednesday, reflecting on the summer breach that triggered a cascade of new questions about AI capabilities. Zoom out: AI's current trajectory needs to continue for only one or two years before reaching what Amodei called "a country of geniuses in a data center," he said in his remarks. That holds massive opportunity, he said, pointing to a discovery announced Wednesday that was led by his company's LLM, Claude: an enzyme system hidden in bacteriophage DNA. Amodei also noted serious risks of the technology, such as misuse by bad actors to create biological weapons or loss of control over advanced systems. Managing that risk depends on global cooperation, he said, calling for an agreement to ban the use of AI to make biological weapons; new evaluation and verification systems; common standards for testing models for risks; and a notification system for global security concerns. Catch up quick: Industry leaders have raised fresh alarms in recent weeks about the rapid advancement of their technology and the need to slow its pace. President Trump , who appeared before the UN General Assembly Tuesday, vowed not to hamstring AI development. The bottom line: Altman warned, "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone." He added, "They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve." item.title: Chicago mayor proposes 12-month moratorium on new data centers
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Chicago could halt new data center development within city limits for a year. Why it matters: Data centers' growing demand for electricity and water could affect residents' utility bills and the environment, and city leaders want more time to study those impacts. The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers. There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city. Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use. What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents." Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers. "The Mayor's proposal risks months if not years of debate and litigation, all while data centers keep building, polluting, and spiking utility bills with zero community input," Conway said in a statement. Conway's ordinance would immediately subject data centers to additional zoning requirements and community and environmental reviews. Zoom out: Chicago wouldn't be alone. At least a half-dozen major U.S. cities, including Seattle, Charlotte, Baltimore, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Oklahoma City, have temporarily halted or restricted new data center development while considering new regulations. At the state level, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has paused new tax incentives for data centers, but has said he doesn't have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on construction. Illinois cities like Bloomington, Carbondale, Effingham, West Chicago and Mattoon have already paused new data center development or expansion. The other side: "As the City of Chicago faces significant and continuing fiscal and budgetary challenges, it's important to recognize that data centers are net revenue generators that provide billions of dollars in economic investment," Data Center Coalition's Brad Tietz said in a statement. "Unfortunately, the Mayor's proposed moratorium sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business." Friction point: Communities across the country are pushing back against proposed data centers over concerns about electricity demand , water use, pollution and other impacts. President Trump has criticized efforts to restrict them, writing on social media: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign." What's next: Both proposals will now make their way through the City Council, setting up a debate over how the city should regulate new data center development.

item.title: Iran president: We have been "victims of terrorism"
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian forcefully rejected President Trump's portrayal of Iran as a source of terrorism at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, insisting instead that Iranians are "victims of terrorism." Why it matters: Pezeshkian used one of the world's biggest diplomatic stages to directly challenge Trump on U.S. soil — as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran rages on. What he's saying: "The United States president described us as terrorists," Pezeshkian said in a roughly 18-minute speech. "We have been the victims of terrorism… Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists." "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," he said. "We live in a world in which the powerful, instead of thinking about humanity, justice, fairness, and democracy, they seem to be the protectors and creators of instability and destruction." Zoom in: Pezeshkian cited attacks that he blamed on the U.S., including strikes that killed children. He pointed to the deaths of more than 150 Iranians at an elementary school in Minab, including more than 120 children. A recent UN report found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. committed a war crime in the strike. While the U.S. has not released findings of an investigation related to the attack, the AP has found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school. Pezeshkian also mentioned the alleged deaths of children playing at a sports hall and an adjacent school after they were struck by a U.S.-made ballistic missile. Between the lines: The same UN report found that Iran's crackdown on protesters likely constituted "crimes against humanity." The report cited tactics including "murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts" as "part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians." What to watch: U.S. and Iranian officials held three hours of indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN on Tuesday, with Trump calling the meeting "very productive" and suggestions a deal remains possible. Iran has downplayed the breakthrough, saying its negotiating position has not changed — underscoring how far apart the two sides remain even as diplomacy continues. item.title: Uber's robotaxi edge: human drivers
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Uber is betting billions on a driverless future, but the secret to making the economics work could be — surprise! — its vast army of human drivers. Why it matters: Uber believes a hybrid network of robots and people can keep its expensive autonomous vehicles busier, and therefore more profitable, than fleets made up entirely of robotaxis. The big picture: Think of a high-tech robotaxi like an airplane: It costs money whether it's carrying passengers or sitting on the ground. The more trips each vehicle makes, the more revenue Uber and its robotaxi partners can squeeze from that expensive asset, offsetting the fixed costs of the technology, vehicle financing, insurance, depot space and other infrastructure. Between the lines: Ride-hailing is a supply-driven business, and robotaxis aren't a substitute for drivers, Uber says — they're an additional form of supply. With greater supply comes lower prices and shorter wait times, which means increased reliability. That stimulates more demand, and ultimately makes the ride-hailing pie bigger. That's Uber's theory. Robotaxi economics remain unproven , Uber's own head of autonomous mobility and delivery, Sarfraz Maredia, tells Axios. It's still early, and no company is making money yet operating them, nor is anyone yet operating them at massive scale. Whether AVs and all that's needed to support a fleet — including charging infrastructure and maintenance — will ultimately be cheaper than today's ride-hailing model "very much has yet to be proven," Maredia says. "The unit economics today have a long way to go." Uber's bet is that its mix of human drivers and AVs will produce better returns. How it works: In a hybrid network — and Lyft has a similar philosophy —AVs would handle the steady "base load" of everyday demand. Human drivers, meanwhile, would provide extra capacity during rush hour, bad weather, concerts and other demand spikes. Maredia points to late nights as an example: Uber can recharge robotaxis when electricity is cheapest while human drivers handle the bar-closing rush. So far , Uber says, robotaxis are taking shorter city-center trips, while drivers get longer, more lucrative ones. "You could argue that the AVs are getting the scraps," CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told Fast Company earlier this year. That flexibility is an advantage , Uber says. A robotaxi operator needs enough cars to handle its busiest periods — leaving expensive AVs sitting idle when demand falls. Uber, by contrast, can size its robotaxi fleet for normal demand and summon more human drivers when needed. Drivers only get paid when they're working, whereas robotaxis cost money even when they're idle. Reality check: Drivers will be displaced eventually, and Uber doesn't argue that point. Part-time drivers who use Uber as a safety net — women, caregivers and lower-income workers — will be disproportionally affected, the company acknowledges. Others will have to work longer or at different times and places to earn the same amount, the company says. But a hybrid network will help ease that transition, it says. By the numbers: Uber says trips are up in Austin and Atlanta, where Waymo AVs are sharing the Uber app with drivers, and driver earnings have stayed consistent. Uber says Waymos on its network in Austin and Atlanta are completing about 30% more trips per vehicle per day than AVs in other major robotaxi markets. Yes, but: Independent research from Gridwise, an app that lets gig drivers track earnings, expenses and mileage, had different findings. It compared earnings for Uber and Lyft drivers in the second quarter with the same period two years ago and found base pay per hour was lower in San Francisco and Los Angeles, where they are competing with Waymo. In Austin, where Waymos are exclusively available on Uber, base pay and gross pay per hour rose less than rideshare drivers in other parts of the country, Gridwise found, suggesting AV growth could already be putting pressure on driver earnings. The bottom line: Humans may make Uber's robotaxi math work. Whether the math works as well for the humans is less certain.

item.title: AI labs are cutting model costs - and it could help them slow down safely
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The shift of the AI frontier toward more powerful, lower-cost models could pave the way for safely slowing development, experts say. Why it matters: Top U.S. startups including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other AI players, have to develop a financially viable path to allow them to slow development. Otherwise financial incentives will be too powerful . Driving the news : The health of the entire U.S. economy now rests in part on the AI boom. Yet the companies at the center of the race are burning far more cash than they take in, and will be for the foreseeable future. Their top executives have also shown unusual solidarity in expressing a desire to slow the pace of model development due to a troubling series of incidents in which rogue AI agents hacked outside companies. Between the lines : To enable a slowdown, in a financial sense, the companies have to find a way to build a value proposition to users that isn't solely rooted in the most mind-blowing intelligence imaginable. That's because remaining at the so-called frontier of capabilities requires a treadmill of never-ending — and mind-boggling spending — to keep up. Slowing the extent of that spending, some of which is used for the computing firepower needed to train new models, would help the companies generate better returns. That wouldn't necessarily threaten spending on computing, data centers and infrastructure such as upgrading the electric grid, according to some economists and AI pros. Those investments will still be needed in order to service demand for AI usage that continues to skyrocket. Catch up quick: Everybody gets a new model this week, and the one thing they all have in common is that they're cheaper than ever without forgoing top intelligence. OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX all emphasized the relatively low costs of their new models this week, as well as their ability to outperform some of their own top systems from only a few months ago. Chinese models including DeepSeek have done the same. DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash, released earlier this month, is now number one on OpenRouter's leaderboard with a 172% spike in usage this week. Reality check: The rationale for the price cuts also goes beyond safety. In a report sent to clients, Citadel Securities found that falling per-token costs are fueling enough additional usage to increase overall AI spending, meaning higher profits for labs even as they cut costs. This paradox is why the AI labs have a rich history of effectively cutting prices for models over time: it increases their customer base and their profits. The bottom line: The race to win on AI costs could be the very thing that allows the labs to enable the slowdown they are seeking.

item.title: Meta's new motto: we care about privacy
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Meta is seeking to make privacy protections a centerpiece of new products including its viral assistant Muse , marking a major shift for a company built on extensive use of customer data. Why it matters: The radical turnaround is an acknowledgment that the winner of AI's new assistant race will have to reassure users that they can turn over their emails, finances, health data and other sensitive information. Without that, a super-intelligent personal agent is essentially useless. Driving the news: Meta, whose privacy policy once allowed it nearly unfettered access to use almost everything people did with Meta AI (in almost any way it wanted), has made a significant shift in recent months to put privacy at the center of its AI strategy. In a 6,500-word August manifesto , CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a broad promise. " We believe that people should have a fully private mode for personal agents where even Meta or any other service provider cannot see or grant access to your information." With Muse, which appears to be on a path to becoming one of the most popular AI hits since ChatGPT, the company is offering all customers their own personal virtual machine. A soon-to-be-available option would ensure that even Meta won't have access to the data. Meta is also readying a similar "private processing" option for interactions with its AI glasses. Small efforts have been underway for more than a year, starting with the addition of incognito chats and private processing , which arrived first in WhatsApp, where Meta also provides end-to-end encryption. More recently, the options have spread to other Meta apps. Yes, but: Customers still have to pay close attention if they want to minimize the amount of data shared with Meta. In Muse, for example, the default setting allows interactions to be used for training the company's AI models, though that can be turned off. And not all of the privacy changes being offered to Muse users apply to those accessing Meta AI in other ways, such as through the Facebook, Instagram or Meta AI apps. Plus, Meta devices continue to spur other types of privacy concerns. "Meta's products that embed microphones and cameras in everyday devices pose serious privacy risks to people just trying to live their lives and go about their day without being recorded or surveilled," Electronic Privacy Information Center executive director Alan Butler told Axios. "Confidential processing doesn't solve the problem of pushing embedded surveillance systems out into the world." The big picture: Meta has spent years building a thriving business based on tapping extensive knowledge about its customers to serve up content and ads that it knows will be right up their alley. Its practices have also drawn lawsuits from a wide range of entities that say Meta designed social media to be addictive and caused harm. How it works: Meta is betting on a new business model to fund Muse, which won't provide the same data for targeted advertising that supports most of the company's services. Muse has $20- and $100-per-month paid tiers for heavy users, but Meta expects the free tier to account for most usage. "We believe that Muse will make you money, and we're standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions," Zuckerberg said. Our thought bubble : There's still a trust gap based on Meta's years of gobbling up nearly all the data it could. That can't be addressed with words, but requires establishing a new track record.

item.title: Scoop: NRSC pleads for $9M to defend three red seats
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The Senate GOP campaign arm is making an extraordinary late ask — $8.9 million, to be exact — for three red states: Alaska, Iowa and Ohio, according to a memo sent Thursday and obtained by Axios. Why it matters: The request is yet another sign of the headwinds facing Republicans. In a good year, they wouldn't be begging for millions to defend states President Trump carried by double digits in 2024. "We need $8.9 million in additional hard dollars to close the media gap and sustain that progress through Election Day," a memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee states. Zoom in: The memo lays out specific fundraising goals for each race, sending donors to joint fundraising accounts and campaigns. $1.2 million in Alaska , where Democratic nominee former Rep. Mary Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in the RealClearPolitics polling average by two percentage points. $4.2 million in Iowa , where Democratic nominee Josh Turek and GOP nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson are separated by less than a percentage point in the RCP polling average. $3.5 million in Ohio , where former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) has built a four-percentage-point lead over Sen. Jon Husted (R) in the RCP polling average. Between the lines: The memo directs donors to candidates' campaigns or joint fundraising committees, which have higher donor limits. The committee has been taking advantage of a Supreme Court ruling to get more advertising at lower prices by coordinating with campaigns. NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) touted this strategy in a closed-door lunch on Wednesday, showing in a chart how it has allowed them to keep up with Democrats' stronger campaign fundraising, according to slides seen by Axios. "The environment remains tough, but these races have improved as the Republican ecosystem has engaged," says the NRSC memo. Zoom out: Cook Political Report this week moved the Senate races in Georgia , Kansas and South Carolina in their ratings toward Democrats. Sabato's Crystal Ball moved Kansas, Michigan and Iowa toward Democrats. Democrats are competitive (at least lean-Republican) in seven seats currently held by Republicans, according to both raters. They only need four to take the majority next Congress. The other side: Democrats have their own late-stage headaches, with Democratic senators calling for a cash infusion for their candidate in Michigan , Abdul El-Sayed — warning that he's getting trounced by outside super PACs. What we're hearing : Republicans are quietly starting to count out North Carolina and Georgia, based on our conversations. Semafor reported millions of dollars in GOP super PAC money were pulled from North Carolina. But the GOP sees a silver lining in New Hampshire and Michigan, where their candidates are making competitive bids to flip Democratic seats. Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is telling candidates to run the race they need to in their state, even if it means breaking with him, Congress, or, in some cases, President Trump. The bottom line: "I'm very realistic about there are political headwinds for us, and so you have to navigate that," Thune told Axios on Wednesday.

item.title: AI's never-before-seen capital grab
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A new analysis of the AI buildout shows its staggering scale: $10.3 trillion in estimated AI infrastructure investment through 2032. That amounts to 3.6% of GDP a year, dwarfing the investment booms that built America's railroads , highways, electric grid and telecom networks. Why it matters: The AI boom has become far too big and too costly for even the largest tech companies to finance alone. This has resulted in trillions of dollars in demand for outside capital — and the potential risks that come along with that, according to new research being presented Friday at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity. Financing the buildout will require tapping bond markets, banks and private credit on a massive scale, adding to the flood of debt competing for investors' money at a time when borrowing costs are already surging. So far, those higher costs appear to be doing little to curb the industry's appetite to build. The knock-on effect: The more capital the buildout absorbs, the greater the potential pressure on borrowing costs elsewhere in the economy. In effect, any other entity that needs capital — from the U.S. government financing its $2 trillion per year deficit to an individual seeking a home mortgage or car loan — is in competition for funds with these hyperscalers. What they're saying: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia Business School professor behind the new paper on how the AI infrastructure boom is being financed, says the industry's appetite for investment remains remarkably resilient to higher rates. "They are so gung-ho to build these things" that even recent rate hikes and historically high long-term yields won't "deter too much of that development," Van Nieuwerburgh told reporters recently. Morgan Stanley estimates that Big Tech will need roughly $2.9 trillion to expand its computing capacity through 2028 — with more than half coming from outside investors, according to the paper. Case in point: Facebook parent Meta chose to finance most of its $30 billion Hyperion data center through outside investors, even though doing so meant paying substantially more to borrow. The project's debt carries an interest rate at least 1 percentage point higher than Meta likely would have paid on its own debt, adding more than $5 billion in costs over the life of the deal, the paper estimates. Threat level: The surge of outside money — much of it from private credit — allows the AI boom to keep scaling. But it spreads possible risks across the financial system, often through financing structures that are harder for investors and regulators to track. The infrastructure would need to generate $3.7 trillion in annual revenue in the next six years to earn a 10% return — roughly 9% of GDP. "The risks have been spreading throughout the financial system," Van Nieuwerburgh said, as the industry taps pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, private credit and other sources of outside capital. "With that expansion comes more complexity, more opacity, and it's becoming difficult to track where the risks are being distributed," he said. "These risks are coming to a pension fund near you, so to speak." What to watch: Van Nieuwerburgh says the influx of outside capital risks allowing the buildout to race ahead of actual demand. "Sooner or later, we're going to have oversupply, just like we do in every real estate cycle, and then the prices will collapse," he said. "I don't see why this time is different." The bottom line: The AI investment boom is now a major force in the broader economy, boosting growth while putting new pressure on capital markets and the financial system. " This AI buildout is by far the largest ... it's 50% larger than the second-largest, which was the railroad buildout," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

item.title: Why Treasury yields are ripping higher
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Treasury yields are soaring, with the 30-year Treasury bond climbing to its highest level since 2004 Thursday. The selloff in bonds started to accelerate Wednesday after a sizzling early report on the economy in September. The big picture: For the bond market, these moves have been big. Bigly even. On Thursday morning, the 30-year yield rose as high as 5.44%. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note was 5.13%. Wednesday's gain of roughly 0.15 percentage point in the 10-year Treasury yield was the biggest since April 2025, when President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement rocked markets. Flashback: Markets heads remember that it was ructions in the bond market — "They were getting yippy ," the president famously said at the time — that prompted Trump to walk back some of the most extreme tariff policies. Yes, but: This time, the dynamics driving the bond market are more complicated, global and difficult to manage. Treasury yields have been moving higher for months on a combination of stronger-than-expected economic activity coupled with uncomfortably high inflation. The surge in data center-related borrowing in the bond market is also pushing up interest rates, as tech borrowers compete with the U.S. Treasury for investor dollars. Case in point: The big driver of Wednesday's surge in yields — which means, remember, that bond prices were falling — was one of the earliest economic reports on the U.S. economy in September. These surveys of corporate purchasing managers suggested booming business in both the U.S. manufacturing and services industries. (JPMorgan economists said they were consistent with a 5% annual run rate for GDP growth.) But they also showed that the prices these companies were paying were soaring as well. (In other words, more inflationary pressures are in the pipeline.) Zoom out: Inflation is anathema for bond market investors as it erodes the value of the interest payments bondholders collect, making them less attractive assets. The September survey data kicked off a wave of selling of Treasurys that rippled through the financial markets. In the money markets — essentially very short-term bond markets — traders began to price in rising odds that Fed will have to pursue a serious cycle of rate hikes to get inflation under control. The markets are now putting more than 50% odds on quarter-point increases at the Fed's October and December meeting. Between the lines: Lurking in the background of the inflation-driven market move is the specter of a U.S. diesel export ban, which the Trump administration is reportedly considering . But there's deep uncertainty about what such a ban would mean for overall inflation. Some industry voices warn that such a ban could actually push prices of other refined products, like gasoline, sharply higher because of the way refineries operate. What they're saying: "The proposed U.S. diesel export ban will not play out as the U.S. administration expects," wrote Susan Bell, an oil analyst with the consulting firm Rystad Energy. "While it may temporarily lower domestic diesel prices, it will cause the prices for all other refined products to soar as U.S. refineries cut run rates to balance their diesel production with the domestic demand." "There is little flexibility to minimize diesel yield without cutting overall refinery throughput," Bell said. The bottom line: The inflationary pressures appear to be building in the economy, which will be a headache both for politicians in the final stretch of the midterm elections and for policymakers like Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh.

item.title: Inside China's mind on AI
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
China is waging a much different war for AI supremacy than the U.S. Why it matters: China is obsessed with state control and adoption. Chinese officials are laser-focused on deep, widespread AI domestic use they can monitor and steer at every level of their economy. By contrast, America is obsessed with developing superior AI faster. Period. The U.S. thinking: The nation first to true super-intelligence wins everything. China and the U.S. agree on three AI certainties: The country with the most powerful AI holds power, sets global standards, and wins the coming decades economically and militarily. From there, the two nations are on different roads. China's 15th Five-Year Plan , released in March, captures their strategy well. AI appears 52 times, 5x more than a half-decade earlier. Computing power gets its own full chapter. Their goal is clear: Integrate AI across 90% of the economy by 2030. America has nothing like this. The bottom line: China doesn't get spooled up about white-collar job loss or humanity-ending rogue AI. The regime is worried most about AI turning against ... the regime. Chen Yixin, China's spy chief, warned this month — in public — about AI's ability to launch public opinion wars and "cognitive warfare against China," threatening "political security, institutional security and ideological security." China's weaknesses China's AI strategy targets some substantial domestic problems they purposely omit in their AI sales pitch. Why it matters: Americans tend to focus on China's growing strength — but much of its AI thinking flows from glaring weakness. 😱 They're staring down: An aging population: China's population has shrunk for four years straight — and is very old. They have nearly as many people over 60 as America has in total. This helps explain their robotics obsession . Very high youth unemployment: China's currently sits at 19% , basically double that of the U.S. — and an angry, young population with powerful AI tools is a threat to power. Poor population outside major cities: This is a huge pain point . Then add in a five-year housing crisis , with prices falling for most people's most valuable asset. Inferior chip production: Nvidia is simply way better than anything they've got. You can't compete on AI with uncompetitive chips — and Huawei, their Nvidia , is way behind despite state-directed help. Export addiction: China is crushing it on exports , often flooding foreign markets with cheap cars, parts and technology. But its domestic economy is sucking wind — strong supply, weak demand. China's strengths China is America's only real AI competition — and, despite its weaknesses, it has some serious, structural advantages. Why it matters: China leads in the physical ingredients for scaling AI: power, materials, robots and cheap models people actually use. These are the key ingredients for turning super-human intelligence into real economic and military power. Think of it this way: If they catch up — or lap us — on AI capabilities and chip production, they're way better positioned to instantly impose and roll it out across society. 🦾 Their edge exists thanks to: Power: Electricity is the biggest bottleneck on America's AI buildout, and China is swimming in it. BloombergNEF estimates China will add almost six times as much generating capacity as the U.S. over the next five years. Vital materials: China dominates the minerals AI hardware runs on. The IEA tracks 20 essential ones for building AI and adjacent tech — and China dominates all but one, usually by huge margins. They have applied export controls to half of them as a way to slow us down. Rolling out robots: This is where AI truly meets the real work. More than half of all industrial robots installed worldwide in 2024 went to China. They dominate us on this one. Better AI will equal better robots. Cheap, widespread adoption: Chinese open-source models are the world's default for developers building cheaply. Five of the six most popular models on OpenRouter , a leading AI marketplace, come from Chinese firms. Land-and-sky autonomy: They're simply crushing us on self-driving cars and self-flying drones. China's DJI alone has over 70% of the global drone market. Understanding China's AI China builds the world's best cheap open-source AI but trails America's most cutting-edge AI by about half a year , on a fraction of the investment. That's the consensus of most AI experts we talk to. Truthfully, there's no rock-solid way to measure it, and every model release resets the estimates. Why it matters: Everyone agrees on this: Chinese models are very good, gaining fast and are much cheaper to use. The four you need to know: Kimi K3 (Moonshot): Widely rated as the best all-around open Chinese model. It's strongest on long, multi-step agentic tasks. Qwen3.8-Max (Alibaba): Also highly regarded and even tops some model rankings. GLM-5.3 (Zhipu / Z.ai): China's coding specialist. Its predecessor scored within a point of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 on a key coding test, at under a fifth of the cost. DeepSeek V4 / V4.1-Flash: Among the cheapest to use . It's MIT-licensed and truly open. The twist: U.S. officials and AI companies accuse Chinese labs of " distillation ," covertly firing millions of questions at American models and training on the answers. Washington has threatened sanctions and blacklisting, but hasn't pulled the trigger. Worth noting: U.S. frontier labs have lately focused far more on building powerful lower-cost models to try to make sure Chinese AI can't undercut them on price. Using it vs. fearing it China is not big on dissent — or public opposition and hand-wringing about the regime's priorities. That helps explain why the Chinese public is far more bullish on AI than America's. Why it matters: They use it, like it and trust it — by wide margins. 80% of Chinese people use AI weekly vs. 54% of Americans. It's in schools, public services and robots in hotels and stores. 84% of Chinese people say AI excites them . That's the highest of any country. Only 38% of Americans say the same. 87% of Chinese people trust AI , compared to just 32% of Americans. And 54% want more of it in daily life. That share is a measly 17% here. Worth noting: Don't over-read it. ChinaTalk, a sharp China tracker, argues the optimism is overstated and masks rising worry about AI wiping out jobs. 📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

item.title: Adapting to extreme heat takes more than changing the clock
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
As extreme heat makes afternoons more dangerous, schools, sports teams and outdoor employers are shifting when — and sometimes whether — people can safely be outside. Why it matters: Adapting to hotter conditions could reshape the American workday while putting a premium on the cooling and energy infrastructure people rely on when outdoor conditions become unsafe. State of play: The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends that employers facing dangerous heat consider moving work to early morning or late afternoon, shortening shifts, rotating workers and reducing strenuous work during the hottest parts of the day. California's new Extreme Heat Action Plan links protecting heat-vulnerable groups, including workers, with expanding access to indoor cooling and strengthening energy systems to reduce grid strain and outages. Oregon's statewide heat-illness prevention rule kicks in when the heat index reaches 80°F, requiring water, shade and acclimatization, with additional measures such as preventive cooldown rest breaks at 90°F, Oregon OSHA told Axios. By the numbers: Oregon OSHA conducted 3,104 inspections addressing heat and issued 408 citations totaling $652,640 in initial penalties from 2022 to 2025, according to data shared with Axios. Case in point: Texas offers a glimpse of the practical tradeoffs that come with reorganizing daily life around heat. Under new statewide rules , schools are moving sports practices to very early or late hours when conditions become dangerous. "Many of our schools have directly adapted their practice times," University Interscholastic League (UIL) athletic director Ray Zepeda told Axios. Moving practices away from peak heat reduces coaches' exposure, Zepeda said, but stretches the workday for coaches and athletic staff who are full-time school employees. "It is increasing their workday," Zepeda said. Reality check: Shifting schedules isn't always enough. Cooling is becoming more important for heat safety at the same time extreme heat can stress the electricity system powering it. "Heat can also stress our electricity grid," California Natural Resources science adviser Andrew Jones said during a recent discussion of the state's updated Extreme Heat Action Plan. A grid failure during a heat event is especially concerning because people rely on electricity for air conditioning and safe indoor spaces, he said. Between the lines: During strenuous outdoor work, workers' own metabolism can become a major source of body heat, Jennifer Vanos, an associate professor at Arizona State University who studies extreme heat and human health, told Axios. Research published this year found rest and self-pacing can help workers manage heat stress. Reducing work intensity or spending less time working can lower heat load, but both can mean less work gets done in that period. "No matter what, somebody is going to pay the price," Vanos said. Vanos points to research suggesting adequate rest and cooling can help workers remain productive while staying safer in hot conditions. The big picture: Changes to working hours are already part of adapting to extreme heat in places like Phoenix, where Vanos said it's "pretty dead" outside during the day. "Part of the shift to being able to live and play and work in these hotter conditions will be having to have certain schedule changes so that everybody can be safer," Vanos said. Overnight heat can also limit how far schedules can shift. Climate change and the urban heat-island effect can keep nighttime temperatures elevated, and in Phoenix "we're reaching some of those limits overnight" for hard physical work, Vanos said. The bottom line: Shifting the clock can buy people relief from extreme heat — but as the number of dangerously hot hours grows, there may be fewer safe hours to shift into.

item.title: The AI doomsday fear hidden in self-improving AI
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Of the various ways experts fear AI could kill us all , one is slowly moving closer to reality: AI learning to make itself unstoppable. Why it matters: Recursive self-improvement, the ability of an AI model to build better versions of itself without human guidance, could make increasingly capable systems harder for humans to control. The RSI threshold doesn't represent danger by itself, but a lack of human control combined with rogue AI agents is a scenario that safety-conscious AI researchers have long feared. Driving the news : Researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI say the process of training new models has grown more automated, coming close to the RSI rubicon. An OpenAI employee told The Information the company has largely automated training new experimental models, with AI systems running experiments as directed by humans and correcting much of their work. Last week, Anthropic shared that its AI training is becoming more automated, with AI leading about 26% of Anthropic's R&D work. AI collaborates on 90% of work, the company says. "AI systems are getting more powerful, and they're increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves," the company said. Reality check: Critics say the milestone is more a function of coding automation than a marker of impending doom or inevitable AI superpowers. While there's been an uptick in troubling AI security incidents in which models outstripped human control, some industry figures see those episodes as evidence of poor internal controls by OpenAI and other companies. Further evidence of that view emerged this week, when the Wall Street Journal reported that independent security researchers used Anthropic's Claude to break into OpenAI in July. Where does RSI come from? Flashback: The concept behind RSI emerged in the 1950s as artificial intelligence became an area of study. British mathematician and statistician Irving John Good described the idea in a 1965 paper : "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control." How RSI could lead to AI doom Threat level: Anthropic has warned RSI "might increase the risks of humans losing control over AI systems." Some researchers theorize that advanced AI could resist shutdown or modification if staying operational helped it accomplish its goals. Researchers into the hack by OpenAI agents into Hugging Face said the agents showed signs of this behavior. In a darker version of this scenario, AI would be competing with humans for resources and power, experts say. Between the lines: Dangerous behavior might not stop with one generation of AI. Anthropic researchers found that some unwanted traits could pass from one model to another through training data, raising concerns that problematic behavior could persist across generations of AI. How close are we to RSI? The big picture: We're not there yet. A new analysis published this week found that AI feedback loops aren't yet hitting the RSI benchmarks. What we're watching: Attempts at building RSI. China's z.AI says they're heading toward RSI, where the models are helping build better infrastructure for better models. Google DeepMind researchers published a framework for "Dream-RSI," a system that recursively improves how an AI agent finds solutions. The bottom line: RSI isn't here yet, but it's a looming issue that's got the AI world on watch. Go deeper: AI's architects say the next era of human history is here

item.title: U.S.-China "red telephone" could bring a Cold War guardrail to AI
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A distinctly Cold War calculus is looming over this week's Trump-Xi summit in Washington, as the U.S. and China weigh an emergency "red phone" for the day AI goes haywire. Why it matters: U.S.-China relations are so brittle that an AI hotline — not a trade pact, strategic slowdown or diplomatic reset — could emerge as the summit's most meaningful outcome. State of play: President Trump has spent the past week lashing out at AI "doomers" and boiling the race down to a single imperative: beat China. Trump has called AI-catastrophe fears a "HOAX" and vowed the U.S. would "not in any way hinder or stifle" AI as it fights to preserve its lead over Beijing. America's leading AI labs largely share Trump's urgency about China, but not his conclusion: many argue the intensity of the race is precisely why global safeguards are needed. The other side: China is every bit as determined to win the AI race, but its leader Xi Jinping — who lands in Washington Wednesday for his first state visit since 2015 — is balancing two competing fears: Falling behind: Xi has no interest in a safety regime that freezes the race with America still ahead. Beijing is pushing cheap, capable open-source models around the world while portraying U.S. chip controls and calls for restraint as a calculated effort to keep China down. Losing control: Xi wants AI powerful enough to transform China's economy, but never so powerful that it slips beyond the control of the Communist Party. Beijing focuses less on Silicon Valley-style extinction scenarios than on nearer-term dangers, like cyberattacks , malicious use and disruptions to critical infrastructure. Zoom in: That narrow overlap is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched Chinese officials this weekend on a "notification mechanism" for AI incidents with national-security implications. The Cold War precedent is the hotline Washington and Moscow established after the Cuban Missile Crisis — a direct channel designed to keep accidents and ambiguity from escalating into nuclear Armageddon. Trump and Xi are expected to discuss shared AI risks when they meet Thursday, while officials are also exploring a formal U.S.-China AI dialogue that could give the crisis channel a more permanent home. Reality check: So far, nobody has publicly defined what would make the red phone ring. In an AI catastrophe — say, a frontier model launches a major cyberattack on critical infrastructure — the first alarm may sound inside a private company rather than a military command center. That gets thorny fast: The lab may know more than the government about what its model is doing, while officials would have to decide how much sensitive information to share before they fully understand the threat themselves. Between the lines: Washington and Beijing already have crisis hotlines, as well as a history of going dark when they're needed most. China suspended military contacts after Nancy Pelosi's 2022 Taiwan visit . Months later, Beijing declined a Pentagon request for a call after the U.S. shot down its surveillance balloon — precisely the kind of tense, ambiguous moments the channels were built to defuse. COVID offered another warning: A cross-border threat that demanded transparency and cooperation instead fueled a bitter U.S.-China blame game over origins, information-sharing and responsibility. The bottom line: The very existence of the proposal is an acknowledgment that AI is no longer just another arena of U.S.-China competition. A serious failure on either side could quickly become a shared crisis.

item.title: New info, new timeline emerges in disappearance of Oceanside mom Angelica Brophy
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Eighty days after emergency room nurse Angelica Brophy disappeared, new investigative details are emerging about the search for the wife and mother of two. Private investigator Anthony Campbell, who was hired by Kaiser Permanente nurses who worked with Brophy, spoke on camera recently about the case for the first time. Campbell said he believes Brophy, 44, is still on Palomar Mountain. Brophy’s car was found at Palomar Mountain Park. “The reason why everything was left in the car, and the way it was left, it was more a goodbye,” Campbell said. Campbell later resigned as a private investigator on the case but continued assisting as a volunteer. “I didn’t want to upset the family, so I did step down and became a volunteer,“ he said. A law enforcement source close to the case also provided NBC 7 with details about what investigators have examined, including Brophy’s marriage, her past and gambling. Related stories Oceanside Aug 21 Volunteer search for missing Oceanside mother Angelica Brophy continues at Palomar Mountain Oceanside Aug 6 One month later, family still searching for missing Oceanside nurse Angelica Brophy Oceanside Jul 15 Timeline released of police investigation into Oceanside mother's disappearance Oceanside Jul 15 Vigil held for missing Oceanside mother, ER nurse Angelica Brophy Oceanside Jul 17 ‘Be prepared for the length of the hike' family of missing Oceanside mom says to search volunteers Missing Persons Jul 13 Search intensifies for missing Oceanside mother near Palomar Mountain The law enforcement source said Brophy had disappeared for a week about 10 years earlier and was found gambling in Las Vegas. According to a timeline on the family’s website, Brophy visited two casinos on the day she went missing. Campbell said he learned more about Brophy’s gambling while investigating her disappearance. “An employee at Harrah’s Casino said she was a high-tier gambler and there every other day to get her free chips to gamble that day,“ Campbell said. The same law enforcement source said investigators looked into difficulties in Brophy’s marriage to her husband, Brent, and concluded he is not a suspect. Investigators also found no foul play. NBC 7 attempted to speak with Brophy’s husband Wednesday, but he was not available. Since Brophy disappeared, more than a dozen searches have covered three specific areas. Friends, relatives, coworkers and strangers have searched trails and Doane Pond in Palomar Mountain Park. Two websites dedicated to finding Brophy feature photos of her with family and members of her hospital team. A piece of a gold necklace or bracelet similar in design to one of Brophy’s was also found along a trail. A law enforcement source close to the case said investigators cannot definitively say it belongs to Brophy. Her brother, Ramon Fabregas, described the item this way: “It’s a common chain that matches her jewelry.” Family members have also confirmed that Brophy stopped at a shop in Temecula and at Pechanga Resort Casino in Temecula on the day she disappeared — two stops that were not previously known. The Brophy family says she was known to visit Pechanga often. After spending two hours there, she went to Harrah’s Resort Southern California in Valley Center, then to Palomar State Park. At the park, her phone pinged one more time not far from the car. After that, it’s not known what happened. Photo provided by the Brophy family The last known photo of Brophy was taken less than 24 hours before she disappeared. It shows her having lunch with family in Westlake, California. Campbell reflected on the photo while discussing his investigation. “It kind of bothers me,” he said. “I’m not somebody who can read faces very well, but it just didn’t appear she was having a good day.” This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego. item.title: Fossils dating back 40-45 million years uncovered in Oceanside
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Pieces of around one dozen fossils were recently found at a construction site in Oceanside. “Walked out and within eight minutes, within the sidewall, saw within minutes a piece of bone sticking out and immediately thought, oh god, we have something,” El Adli said. Helix Environmental Planning Principal Paleontologist Dr. Joseph El Adli made the discovery a few weeks ago. The city of Oceanside is not releasing the exact location of the construction site because they want to “protect public safety and the integrity of the site,” but El Adli shared that the bones were found in what’s known as the Santiago Formation, which is a rock unit 40-45 million years old. “We had about 6 feet of rock to dig down by hand to get to the bone itself from what we had found,” El Adli said. The bones could belong to one of two animals from 40 to 45 million years ago during a time in San Diego history where it was tropical, more humid, and more of a forest environment during the Eocene Epoch. The San Diego Natural History Museum already preserves fossils from both those animals. Dr. Tom Deméré, the San Diego Natural History Museum Curator of Paleontology, showed NBC 7 those remains, which were also found in the Santiago Formation. “This is a, well, this is a partial lower jaw of a Brontotheriidae,” Deméré showed us. It’s also called a Thunder Beast, which El Adli described looking like a rhino, massive in size with a Y-shaped bony horn on the nose. “This is a lower jaw, again, broken off an Amynodontidae,” Deméré said. “It has different style teeth.” This animal is known as a Swamp Rhino. Its body is more hippo-shaped, and a part of an extinct family of large-bodied herbivores. Upon being discovered, the fossils were covered in plaster jackets and sent to a lab where they will be cleaned and eventually reveal what these bones belong to. From the bones that El Adli did find, from ribs to limbs to other fragments ranging from 3 inches to a foot, he believes the animal probably lived in a flood plane. ”To me this indicates that this animal, 45 million years ago, died, and then was sitting on the surface for a very long time,” El Adli said. While these bones date back more than 40 million years, Deméré says the oldest fossils in the coastal area in San Diego County are about 140 million years old. He calls it a blink of the eye when you think about the world as 4.6 billion years old. “What’s beneath your feet is crazy,” Deméré said. It’s what El Adli and Deméré say can tell us so much about the past. “We’re protecting our past; we’re protecting our history. If we don’t know, we’re never gonna learn these things are here, we’re never gonna know what San Diego was like 40 million years ago,” El Adli said. “How we got to be who we are now – it’s all wrapped up in this history.” Looking ahead to the winter, both El Adli and Deméré said the potential for heavy rain could mean more fossils uncovered across the area. item.title: Mold concerns keep Monarch School students at temporary campuses
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Students at Monarch School in San Diego will remain at temporary campuses at least through next week after air quality testing found mold at the Barrio Logan school. When the school, which serves youth who are homeless, temporarily closed on Aug. 28, all 170 K-12 students were relocated to nearby schools. Younger students were relocated to Perkins, while older students went to the South County Regional Education Center in National City. The San Diego County Office of Education asked parents to provide permission for the relocation through December in case remediation takes that long. The Monarch School Project (MSP) provided the following updates on the closure: Following thorough analysis, Monarch School Project has identified areas within the building requiring remediation and is actively working with qualified experts and remediation professionals to address these conditions. The health and safety of our students, families, staff and broader community remain our highest priority. We are continuing to work closely with a team of experts and the San Diego County Office of Education to review the building, determine appropriate next steps and develop timelines for remediation and the eventual return to the facility. Areas of the building will be cleared for access only following the guidance and upon authorization of qualified experts. We understand the uncertainty is difficult for families, and we will continue to share updates as more information becomes available. The San Diego County Office of Education rents the building from MSP for instruction and also provided an update: We have been communicating regularly with parents and families and in an abundance of caution and to reduce the number of permission forms needed during this time, we extended the date range on the permission slips through December. We will remain at Perkins K-8 and the South County Regional Education Center at least through next week, however, SDCOE is actively exploring longer-term solutions that will better meet the needs of our staff members and families. We will not resume operations at the school until our own testing has shown that the facility is safe. In the meantime, we remain focused on ensuring our students and staff have a clean and comfortable environment for teaching and learning. We’re grateful for the understanding and flexibility our school community has shown during this time. Eighth grader, Eva Gonzalez, said the move has significantly changed her schedule a lot and she now has a longer commute to school. “I ride the bus all the way over there. I have to wake up earlier than I already normally wake up to get to school, and I have to like be fast about it,” she said. Gonzalez said mold has been a concern at Monarch for years. “I feel like I have been exposed to mold because I’ve been here since kindergarten, so I’ve been here for a long, long time. I’ve been, like, around it for like, a minute, so I don’t know why they’re taking action now instead of before, you know?” she said. Parents are also seeking more communication about the situation. Jessica Cortes, Gonzelez’s mother, has three other children who attend the school. “They’re not really giving us a lot of information. And I just said parents could volunteer to help out the situation and sign a waiver for us to help clean the problem,” Cortes said. Cortes said she would be willing to help with the mold remediation herself because of what the school means to her children. “This is their community. This is their safe zone. This is their second home. As long as my kids feel comfortable and safe, I’m willing to volunteer,” Cortes said. This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego.
